title: Throw an error on createVNode with using `innerHTML` and `children` at the same time

judge.reasoning: Patch A changes runtime behavior at the point where a crash or corruption can happen. In `patchElement`, when `innerHTML`/`textContent` goes from set to unset, the old children's DOM nodes have already been overwritten. Patching them in place therefore operates on nodes that no longer exist, which is the kind of failure the issue reports. A unmounts the old array children, which also runs component unmount hooks, and then mounts the new text or array children fresh. It also switches the guard from a truthiness check to `!= null`, so an empty-string `innerHTML` is handled correctly. Its tests cover the exact issue scenario (`innerHTML: undefined` with text children) and several transitions: undefined to html to undefined, empty string to undefined, array children, component children with an unmount count, and `textContent`. These transition tests would plausibly fail before the change, and an SSR test checks that undefined values fall back to children. Patch B only adds a dev-mode warning when a non-nullish `innerHTML`/`textContent` is combined with children. It explicitly does not warn for nullish values, which is the issue's case, and it makes no runtime change, so the reported error and the expected behavior (use children when `innerHTML` is undefined) are not addressed. B's tests only check warnings. On correctness, the primary criterion, A clearly wins.

title: suspense.resolve() is called without a pending branch.
issue_md:
### Vue version

3.2.45

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://codesandbox.io/s/vue-router-playground-forked-w9164p?file=/src/pages/Page2.vue

### Steps to reproduce

Create an application with vue and vue-router and the suspense component.

When creating a page, during the setup function navigate to another page (in my case this is how I handle an error) than this error is triggered.



### What is expected?

Just no error message from vue / Suspense.

### What is actually happening?

I get the following error message:

`
suspense.resolve() is called without a pending branch.
`

Nevertheless I can keep on using the application without any problems. I just want to get rid of the error message.

_No response_

_No response_

title: the div which has the ref attribute inside the v-for, when I v-if toggle them, the ref value.length increase more and more

judge.reasoning:
The bug happens when a keyed element is a direct child of a stable v-for. `:key` forces the element into a block, so `buildProps` skips adding NEED_PATCH. `transformFor` then demotes the block to a plain vnode with no patch flag. The vnode is therefore missing from the fragment's dynamicChildren, and the unmount path never resets its ref, directives or vnode hooks.

Patch B removes `!shouldUseBlock` from the NEED_PATCH condition. Every block with ref/hook/directive and flag 0 now gets 512. This is minimal and fixes the reported static-ref case. It is mostly harmless for real blocks, which explains the snapshot churn. However, it leaves two gaps:
- `hasRef` is still only set after the early return for const/setup bindings. A keyed v-for child with `:ref="setupConstFn"` still gets no NEED_PATCH and is still dropped from tracking. That is the same bug class, and the issue explicitly compares against function refs.
- Elements that needed a block for ordering (`@vue:before-update` or runtime directives with children) are still silently demoted. They are now tracked, but beforeUpdate can fire after the children update.

Patch A addresses the root cause more completely:
- It moves the `hasRef` detection before the const-binding early return, so setup-const function refs are covered.
- It records `needsPatch` on the VNodeCall and applies NEED_PATCH only when vFor actually demotes the node. Real blocks are left untouched, so there are no snapshot changes.
- It adds `isBlockRequired`, so before-update hooks (now matched camelized as well) and directives with children stay blocks inside stable fragments, preserving hook ordering.

A's tests cover compiler flags for static ref, directives, vnode hooks and the const function ref, plus block preservation. They also include runtime tests for ref-array clearing, function-ref null calls, unmounted hooks and beforeUpdate ordering. B's tests are solid but cover only the static-ref, directive and hook cases.

A is more complex, but the added logic is targeted and well tested. It holds up across more of the scenarios this bug class implies, so A is the better fix.

title: defineProps options object loses properties when using generics

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the same root cause the same way. They replace the conditional `PropMethod<T>` with an unconditional function-like constructor type. That stops `PropType<T>` from becoming a deferred conditional when `T` is a type parameter, and that deferral is what caused `RequiredKeys`/`OptionalKeys` to drop non-required props. The difference is in `InferPropType`.

Patch A keeps the `unknown extends V ? keyof V extends never ? ...` chain. It only swaps the inner `D` for `unknown extends D ? V : D`. When `V` is a generic `T`, `unknown extends V` stays deferred, so the result is still an unresolved conditional type. Patch A relies on TypeScript treating that deferred conditional as assignable to `T` when both branches are. That probably passes `expectType`, but users still get an opaque conditional type rather than `T`, and it is a less direct fix.

Patch B adds an earlier check: `[T] extends [PropType<any> | { type: PropType<any> }]`. For an explicit runtime type it returns `V` directly. Because the prop-options object type is not itself a generic object type, this resolves eagerly to a clean `T`. That is the more robust result.

There is a modest risk that B's short-circuit changes behaviour for explicit-type props where `V` is `unknown` and a default supplies `D`. That is an edge case, and the existing suites would likely catch it.

On tests, B is clearly stronger. It covers exactly the issue's three shapes (bare `PropType<T>`, `{type}`, `{type, required}`) plus defaults, arrays, union constructors, function props with generic args, Boolean/String alongside generics, readonly-ness and unknown-key errors. It covers both `defineProps` and `defineComponent` (`setup` and `this`), and it also checks `ExtractPropTypes`, `ExtractPublicPropTypes` and `ExtractDefaultPropTypes`. A's test is narrower: it constrains `T extends Record<string, any>` and checks only a few cases plus assignability.

Scope is comparable. Overall B gives a cleaner inferred type and much broader regression coverage.

title: Clearing `select`'s value in change handler behaviour changed since 3.4.15 via webdriver

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the same root cause. Since the select performance change, `updated` skips `setSelected` whenever `_assigning` is true. So if the model changes again in the same tick (for example, reset to null in an `@change` handler), the DOM is never resynced.

Patch A records the assigned value and resyncs when `toRaw(value) !== toRaw(_assignedValue)`. That covers the reported case: a single select reset to null, or a multiple select reassigned to a new array. However, it relies on reference identity. If the handler mutates the emitted array or Set in place (for example `value.pop()`, `value.length = 0` or `set.delete(x)`), the reference is unchanged. A then still skips the resync and the DOM stays stale. That is the same class of bug the issue describes, so A only partly closes it. A's two tests are reasonable and would fail before the fix.

Patch B stores a snapshot of the pending value, copying `selectedVal` for array models. In `updated` it compares that snapshot to the current model by content: `looseEqual` for single and Array values, and a membership check for Sets. It also detects a `multiple` flip, clears the pending state after the first `updated`, and uses try/finally plus an identity check so a throwing assigner cannot leave stale state. As a result it handles both reset-by-reassignment and reset-by-mutation, while still skipping redundant DOM writes when nothing changed, which preserves the purpose of the original performance optimization.

B's tests are broader and meaningful. They include the issue's change-handler reset, in-place Array and Set mutation, Set override, duplicate option values, and write-counting tests confirming no extra `selected` writes in the common case. B is more code, but it is coherent and low-risk, and the extra comparison helper is clearly named. On correctness, B is more robust within the issue's scenario space, so B wins.

👋 sorry I can only reproduce this myself when acting on chrome with webdriver, but I have narrowed it down a lot

the basic premise is we have a strange select that clears its value on change, exampled in the repo link

The bug occurs when _webdriver_ clicks the `select` and clicks one of the `option`s within the value does not get cleared afterwards. If I click in the page myself it clears properly.

The value of the select afterwards should be null

it is whatever was selected last, ie 0 or 1

title: Transition should sniff for teleport in custom components

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause. Each makes a component whose root is a Teleport forward the Transition hooks to the Teleport's inner child: at initial render in renderComponentRoot, and on later hook updates through setTransitionHooks recursing into the component subTree.

Patch A does this with an `isTeleport(...) ? getInnerChild(...) || ... : ...` check repeated at two call sites. It reuses getInnerChild/findNonCommentChild, which reads `c.type` on every child. Teleport children built with h() are not normalized yet at renderComponentRoot time, so a null or false entry (e.g. `h(Teleport, {to}, [null, h('div')])`) would throw a TypeError.

Patch B puts the Teleport handling inside setTransitionHooks as its own TELEPORT branch. That covers the component-subTree recursion, HOC chains and any other caller in one place. Its getTeleportInnerChild filters out non-vnode children first, which avoids the crash above. B also adds isTransitionableRoot so the dev warning is suppressed only when the Teleport actually wraps an element. If the child is missing it falls back cleanly.

On tests, B's unit tests are stronger. They check enter and leave hook calls with the right elements. They check that the element stays in the teleport target until leave completes, and they cover the HOC wrapper, null/false children and out-in mode, plus the absence of warnings. All of these would fail before the fix.

A's e2e test does cover the issue scenario well. Its unit tests are thinner, though: one KeepAlive test unrelated to the issue, one empty-Teleport test and one hook-update test.

Overall, B is more robust in implementation and test coverage with comparable scope.

title: defineCustomElement can accidentally override members of the Element prototype

judge.reasoning:
The issue's main complaint is that Vue silently overrides native Element members like `tagName`. It explicitly accepts a warning as a remedy. Patch A adds a dev-only warning when a declared prop name already exists on the element's prototype. The prop/property behavior stays exactly as before, so existing code keeps working. Its tests cover the reported `tagName` case, a reflected native property (`id`), and a native method (`hasAttribute`) set from a Vue render. Each asserts the warning, and those assertions would fail without the change.

Patch B goes further. It stops defining accessors for any prop that collides with something in the prototype chain, routes Vue-rendered bindings for those props through a new patchProp branch, and also changes `_applyExpose` to skip anything in the prototype chain. That stops the override, but it is a silent breaking change for common prop names like `title`, `hidden`, `lang`, `dir` and `id`. JS code doing `el.title = someObject` used to set the Vue prop. Now it hits the native setter, which stringifies the value and only reaches the prop indirectly through attribute reflection. For non-reflected native members it doesn't reach the prop at all. The expose change similarly alters existing behavior for names like `focus`. The extra patchProp branch adds complexity and runs before the existing `.`/`^`/shouldSetAsProp logic, which adds risk on a hot path. B's tests are thorough, but they lock in this riskier semantic change.

Patch A satisfies the issue's ask with minimal risk. Patch B's broader redesign introduces regressions for existing users, so A is the better fix.

I know this is user error, but I was surprised that Vue let me.

title: Custom directive's unmounted event is not triggered on v-for element

judge.reasoning:
Root cause: in a stable v-for (constant source), the child is first forced into a block, either by a dynamic `:key` or by a before-update hook / custom directive with children. Because it is a block, buildProps skips NEED_PATCH. transformFor then demotes it to a plain vnode, so it is missing from the parent's dynamicChildren and its directive/ref/vnode-hook unmount is skipped. Both patches restore NEED_PATCH on demotion, so both fix the reported `:key` + directive case. Patch A carries the decision from buildProps itself. It adds `needsPatch` and `isBlockRequired` on the VNodeCall, so the vFor transform reuses the same analysis instead of duplicating it. A also sees the deeper problem. When an element was made a block so that before-update hooks run before its children update, demoting it to a plain vnode breaks that ordering. Nested dynamic children get collected into the fragment's dynamicChildren ahead of the parent and are patched before the parent's beforeUpdate. A keeps such elements as blocks (`isBlockRequired`). It also handles the camelized `vue:beforeUpdate` spelling. Its runtime tests check this ordering, and they check unmount of directive hooks, vnode hooks, static ref arrays and setup-const function refs. Patch B re-scans the AST props in vFor with a hand-written mirror of buildProps' condition. That copy is fragile and partly odd: it checks `on` args starting with `vnode`, and only static args. B also demotes before-update/directive-with-children blocks, which keeps the hook-ordering regression. Its compiler test even asserts that `

hi

` becomes a non-block vnode. B's integration tests are good for the reported scenario but never exercise ordering with nested dynamic children. Overall, A fixes the root cause more robustly and preserves the block semantics. It has broader, meaningful tests and only a modest increase in scope.

title: Vue is not catching errors on server side in SSR when using async child setup

judge.reasoning: The issue has two parts: the child's template should not be rendered once its async setup has thrown, and the error should reach the parent's onErrorCaptured. Patch B fixes this at the root. Its runtime-core change re-throws from the SSR async-setup `.catch` after `handleError`, so the error still reaches errorCaptured or the app errorHandler. The server renderer then sees the rejection, sets `setupFailed`, and emits a `<!---->` placeholder instead of calling `renderComponentSubTree`. This also skips serverPrefetch on the failed instance. It matches client-side behavior, where a failed async component leaves a comment placeholder, and it never touches incomplete setup state. Its tests check the right things: the subtree is not rendered, the render function is never called, siblings still render, errorCaptured is called exactly once, and the spurious 'missing template' warnings are gone from the existing Suspense tests. Patch A treats only the symptom. It still renders the child's template with missing state, then catches the resulting TypeError in `renderComponentSubTree` and routes it through `handleError`. Its own test confirms this: two errors are captured, the real one plus a "Cannot read properties of undefined" error, and a 'Property foo was accessed during render' warning appears. That is exactly the behavior the issue complains about, now caught rather than prevented. Patch A also changes SSR render-error handling for every component (render errors now go to handleError, followed by a Promise.reject conversion), which is a broader behavior change with more risk. Patch B is the more correct, root-cause fix with better-targeted tests.

issue_md:
### Vue version

3.5.13

### Link to minimal reproduction

[Vue SFC Playground](https://play.vuejs.org/#__SSR__)

### Steps to reproduce

Just open a link and you will see errors when SSR is ON.
When SSR is OFF everything works as expected.

Also, commeting the line with top-level await (making `Comp.vue` a sync component) will also work fine both with and without SSR.

### What is expected?

In SSR mode the page is expected to be blank white for 1 second and then display error message from `App.vue`.
This works as expected with SSR turned off.

Basically `onErrorCaptured` should be triggered, child setup and `<template>` render immediately stopped and error message from parent component shown.

### What is actually happening?

In SSR mode the page is blank for 1 second but then it tries to render the `<template>` of `Comp.vue` using the data that might not even exist (because it appears in `setup` after throwing error).

And even if it manages to render `<template>` correctly, it still does not trigger `onErrorCaptured` in `App.vue` and do not switch to show error message.

### Any additional comments?

I am building a custom rendering package built on top of Vue and it heavily uses structures like these:

```vue
 // Wrappers are supposed to catch ALL errors and throws in child <Block /> and show nice error message

<BlockWrapper>
    <Block ... />
</BlockWrapper>

<BlockWrapper>
    <Block ... />
</BlockWrapper>

<BlockWrapper>
    <Block ... />
</BlockWrapper>

...
```

Because of this bug OR my misunderstanding of how to handle async errors in Vue 3, even when thrown it still tries to render child block's `<template>` even with missing data (because setup is stopped executing), throws on reading properties of non-existing objects and the whole Nuxt page breaks.

Please, don't tell me this is a no-fix. It would be a disaster... 😭

title: $el of templateRef points to comment VNode instead of first real child of component

judge.reasoning:
Both patches find the same root cause. In dev builds, root-level template comments turn the root into a fragment marked DEV_ROOT_FRAGMENT, so `vnode.el` is the fragment's start anchor rather than the single real element. Both fix it the same way: walk component subTrees and use `filterSingleRoot` on DEV_ROOT_FRAGMENT nodes, returning the resolved element only when such a fragment was actually found. Otherwise existing `$el` semantics, including multi-root anchors, are unchanged.

Patch A puts this logic in a shared helper, `getComponentRootEl`, in componentRenderUtils. It applies the helper everywhere a user-facing element is derived from a component vnode:
- `$el` on the public instance.
- `setRef` for functional components, where a template ref resolves to `vnode.el` and has the same bug.
- Compat `vnode.elm`.

This covers more of the issue's user-facing surface ("templateRef points to comment"), not just `$el` on stateful components.

Patch A's tests are well targeted and would fail before the change:
- Single-root with a comment, including a reactive update that checks `$el` stays stable.
- Nested components that both have root comments.
- A regression guard that multi-root components still return the fragment anchor.
- A functional-component ref.
- A compat test using a real template with a comment, which exercises the actual compiler output.

Patch B fixes only `$el`. It adds Suspense activeBranch traversal and tests for mounting-time safety and unresolved async roots. That hardening is reasonable but sits beyond the issue's ask. Patch B misses the functional-component template-ref case, which shows the same symptom.

On craft, Patch A's shared helper is cleaner and reusable. Patch B's two-function split (`resolveDevRootEl` returning `undefined` as a sentinel, plus `getDevRootFragmentEl`) is slightly more convoluted.

Overall, Patch A is the more complete fix and has stronger tests.

### Steps to reproduce

Hi, I just spent some hours debugging a very strange behavior when accessing the underlying element of a component ref by using `templateRef.$el`. The component I placed the template ref on had only one root level `<div>` inside its template, however there was a comment above it. It looks like this leads to the element being referenced by the template ref being the VNode of this comment instead of the `<div>` element.

Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the [Playground](https://play.vuejs.org/#__PROD__)
2. Open the console and see that the element referenced by `childRef.value.$el` is a text VNode
3. Click on the text "Test" in the preview (Nothing should be logged to the console)
4. Go into the component "Child.vue" and remove the comment in line 2
5. After a hot reload (or manual one) `childRef.value.$el` should point to the div element as logged to the console. Clicking on the text "Test" in the preview should now also log "Clicked Test" to the console

### What is expected?

I would expect `templateRef.$el` to point to the first real element inside the component excluding comments.

### What is actually happening?

`templateRef.$el` points to a VNode for the comment inside the components template.

title: Preserve input values entered during hydration

judge.reasoning: Both patches use the same root-cause approach: during hydration the element is already attached in `created`, so each compares the live DOM value against the server-rendered default and, if they differ, writes the DOM value into the model instead of overwriting it in `mounted`. They differ in coverage. Patch B only handles `type === 'text'` inputs and textareas. Password, email, search, tel, url and number inputs still get reset, as do checkboxes, radios and selects. The issue is about forms in general, so many common fields stay broken. Patch A handles text-like inputs of every type, including a sanitization-aware comparison for range and color inputs and support for the .trim and .number modifiers. It also handles textarea, checkbox (including true-value/false-value and array/Set models, with a pending-model map so several boxes sharing a collection combine correctly), radio, and select (single and multiple, including correct default-index logic for selects with no `selected` attribute). It deliberately skips custom elements. Patch A's tests are thorough: each element type, the modifiers, the unchanged-by-user case, and false-positive guards for browser-sanitized values and selects with no matching option. Patch B adds a single text-input test. Patch A is more complex, notably the `pendingCheckboxModels` mechanism, but the complexity is targeted and tested, and the refactors (`assignChecked`, `assignSelected`) keep existing behavior. On correctness breadth and tests, Patch A is clearly better.

title: v-model on <select multiple> uses stale collection type after switching between Array and Set

judge.reasoning: Both patches apply the same root-cause fix. They store the current model value on the element in `created` and refresh it in `beforeUpdate`, and the change listener calls `isSet(el._modelValue)` at event time instead of using the stale `isSetModel` captured at creation. Correctness is equivalent: both handle Array->Set and Set->Array switches and keep `el.multiple` semantics unchanged. Both tests would fail before the fix and pass after, since the first change event after a runtime switch would emit the old type. Patch A's test is slightly stronger. After each switch it also asserts that the DOM `selected` state was synced to the new model before the user interaction, and its interaction modifies only one option, which mirrors a real user action. Patch B forces both options' selected states manually and skips those checks. On craft, Patch A is clearly better. It adds `_modelValue?: any` to the `ModelDirective` element type, matching how `_assigning` is declared, and adds a short explanatory comment. Patch B uses repeated `(el as any)` casts with leading-semicolon statements, which is less consistent with the surrounding typed code. Scope is minimal and equal for both. Patch A wins on test thoroughness and type-safe consistency.

### Vue version

3.5.39

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#__PROD__

### Steps to reproduce

1. Bind a `<select multiple v-model>` to an Array.
2. Switch the bound value to a Set at runtime.
3. Interact with the select again.
4. The emitted model becomes an Array again.
5. Switching back from Set -> Array shows the same stale-type behavior in reverse.

The current collection type should be respected after the model switches at runtime.


### What is actually happening?

The change handler keeps using the collection type captured when the directive was created, so the first user interaction after a runtime Array/Set switch emits the old type.

title: Scoped slot transforms array argument if rendered conditionally

judge.reasoning:
Both patches find the same root cause: the compiler injects the v-if/v-for branch `key` into slot props via `mergeProps`, which turns an array `v-bind` value into an object. Both fix it the same way, by passing the key as a new 6th argument to `renderSlot`, so the slot receives the props unchanged. Both fix the reported v-if case.

**Why A is better on correctness:** A also handles a closely related path that B misses. When a slot outlet with `v-bind` sits inside v-for, `buildProps` calls `pushRefVForMarker`. That merges `{ref_for: true}` into the slot props and reshapes an array the same way. A skips the marker for `ElementTypes.SLOT` and adds a test confirming that `ref="foo"` on a slot still keeps `ref_for`. Under B, `<slot v-for="list in lists" v-bind="list"/>` still passes an object instead of the array.

**Scope:** A is narrow. It only reroutes the key when the slot props are a single v-bind expression, which is the case that breaks. Plain-object props keep the existing `{ key: 0 }` output, so existing snapshots are unchanged. B reroutes every injected slot key, including slots with no props. That changes existing codegen to `{}, undefined, undefined, 0` and rewrites existing tests and snapshots. B also adds a snapshot to `transformElement.spec.ts.snap` for a vFor test, which looks like misplaced churn.

**Where B is slightly better:** B keeps the old precedence where a user-provided `props.key` wins over the branch key, both at runtime and in the compiler via `hasProp`. A lets the compiler key override a `key` inside the v-bind object, a minor behavior change.

**Tests:** A adds end-to-end runtime tests in `packages/vue` covering v-if toggling, keyed template v-for with element reuse after reordering, and slot v-for, all checking `Array.isArray(props)`. B adds only compiler and unit-level tests.

Overall, A fixes more of the actual bug class with less churn and has stronger tests.

Pass an array as the sole argument to the slot ### What is expected? Array is rendered normally. If you render items of that array in `v-for` loop, you only see items inside that array ### What is actually happening? Array is transformed into object. Items and their indexes are staying the same, `key` field is added ### System Info ```shell ``` ### Any additional comments? `key` attribute is generated by the compiler for the slot rendered with `v-if`. While this is not explicitly mentioned in documentation, one can assume that the expectation is that `slotProps` is always an object, as this is what will be passed to the slot if you use multiple `v-bind` directives on the slot. This issue is rather pointing out the difference in behavior of the slot when `v-if` is present or not present.

### Vue version

3.5.39

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://stackblitz.com/edit/vitejs-vite-qfkzyzwp?file=leak.mjs

### Steps to reproduce

- download the reproduction from stackblitz (won't work there, needs to be run locally)
- run `pnpm i && pnpm leak`
- see the heap size & alive app instances grow with each request after the single failed render

The script renders 500 fresh SSR apps, which all get garbage-collected. Then renders **one** app whose slot content throws, then renders 500 more identical healthy apps, which will never be garbage collected afterwards.

A dynamic component `<component :is>` with a `<slot />` is needed for this to reproduce.

Card

```vue
<script setup>
    defineProps({ tag: { type: String, default: 'div' } })
</script>

<template>
    <component :is="tag" class="card">
        <slot />
    </component>
</template>
```

app:

```vue
<script setup>
    defineProps(['payload'])  // one request renders with `payload: null` → throws
</script>

<template>
    <main>
        <Card>{{ payload.title }}</Card>
    </main>
</template>
```

### What is expected?

A failed `renderToString` should not affect subsequent renders and all apps rendered after it should get garbage collected.

### What is actually happening?

Every app created after the single failed render is kept in memory forever.

```
after 500: created=500 finalized=500 alive=0 heap=20.6MB

--- phase 2: 500 healthy renders (identical to phase 1) ---
after 500: created=1001 finalized=500 alive=501 heap=29.0MB

FINAL: created=1001 finalized=500 alive=501
```

title: SSR hydration warning: dynamic props on SVG elements are patched as properties instead of attributes

judge.reasoning: Both patches fix the root cause the same way. In hydrateElement, they work out the element's own namespace from el.namespaceURI ('svg', 'mathml' or undefined) and pass it to patchProp instead of undefined. runtime-dom's shouldSetAsProp then sends SVG props to setAttribute. Both use the element's own namespace rather than getContainerType, so <foreignObject> is correctly treated as SVG. On correctness they are essentially equal. B also passes the namespace in the onClick fast path, which is harmless and consistent. B also null-checks namespaceURI, which avoids A's non-null assertion. The real difference is the tests. A's first test hydrates a plain <svg> in jsdom without making width, height or viewBox read-only. jsdom's SVGSVGElement does not expose these as settable properties, so `key in el` is likely false and setAttribute is used either way. That test would probably pass even without the fix. Only A's foreignObject test, which defines a getter, would actually fail before the fix. B adds a helper that makes the relevant SVG properties getter-only, which mimics how browsers behave. It then tests <svg> and a nested <rect> in dev mode, asserting no 'Failed setting prop' warning. It also covers production mode, <foreignObject> with an HTML child that is still patched as a property, and teleported SVG content. Each of these would fail before the fix and pass after it, and they directly reproduce the issue's symptom. The shared helper (getElementNamespace) is a clean, documented addition next to the existing namespace helpers. B wins on test quality and slightly on craft.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Open the reproduction.
2. Open the browser devtools **Console**.
3. Observe the `[Vue warn]: Failed setting prop …` error logged during hydration.

### What is expected?
During hydration, dynamic props on SVG (and MathML) elements `width`, `height`, `viewBox`, etc.  should be patched as **attributes** (via `setAttribute`) exactly as they are during normal client-side rendering. Hydration should be silent.

Since 3.5.39, dynamic props on SVG elements are patched as **DOM properties** during hydration, which throws for read-only SVG IDL properties:

```
    at patchDOMProp
    at patchProp
    at hydrateElement
    at hydrateNode
    at hydrateSubTree
    at <App>
```

Nothing is visually broken but the console is flooded with warnings.

title: EffectScope stop() causes runtime crash (Cannot read properties of undefined) when dynamic scope cleanup mutates parent.scopes array during traversal

judge.reasoning:
The source changes are functionally identical. Both patches copy `this.scopes` with `slice()` before iterating in `pause()`, `resume()` and `stop()`, and both also copy `this.effects` in `resume()`. That fixes the root cause the issue describes: the parent loop used a cached length while a child's cleanup removed a sibling from `parent.scopes`. The only source difference is that Patch B adds brief comments explaining why the copies are needed, which helps future readers.

On correctness, they tie.

The tests are where the patches differ.

Patch A adds two tests, and both would fail before the fix:
- A child's cleanup stops a sibling scope, which hits the undefined `.stop` crash in `stop()`.
- A sync watcher stops a sibling watcher during `resume()`, which hits the undefined `.resume` crash on effects.

Patch B covers the same core scenario with stronger assertions:
- It checks that both children's dispose callbacks ran exactly once.
- It checks that all scopes are inactive and that `parent.scopes` is emptied.

Patch B also adds `resume()` scenarios Patch A does not cover:
- A resumed effect stops a sibling child scope. This exercises the scopes loop in `resume()` and verifies that a later sibling, `child3`, is still resumed and runs its queued effect.
- A resumed effect stops its own scope.
- A `once` watcher stops itself during resume. This verifies that the remaining effects are still resumed and stay reactive afterwards.

These tests exercise each changed loop more thoroughly. They also assert that no sibling is skipped, not just that nothing throws.

Scope is equivalent. Patch B wins on test thoroughness and slightly on craft (explanatory comments).

issue_md:
### Vue version

3.5.28

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#

### Steps to reproduce

Open the reproduction link.
Click the "Trigger сrash" button.
Observe the output status on the screen or check the browser console.

### What is expected?

The parent scope should stop all its children successfully. When a child scope stops a sibling scope during the cleanup phase, the parent traversal loop should handle the array mutation gracefully without throwing errors.

### What is actually happening?

The application crashes with the following error: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'stop')

This happens because EffectScope.stop loops over this.scopes using a cached length l. During iteration, one child's onScopeDispose calls stop() on its sibling. The sibling removes itself from the parent's scopes array, reducing the array size. When the parent loop continues to the cached index l, it tries to access an element out of bounds (which is undefined), causing the runtime crash.

### System Info

```shell
System: OS: macOS, Browser: Chrome, Node: v20.19.5
```

### Any additional comments?

The bug lies in packages/reactivity/src/effectScope.ts.

Inside EffectScope, the methods pause(), resume(), and stop() loop over this.scopes using a cached length without accounting for array mutations. Creating a shallow copy of the array before iterating (e.g. const scopes = this.scopes.slice()) safely resolves the issue.

title: hydrateOnVisible: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'nodeType') when the SSR node is detached before the IntersectionObserver callback fires

judge.reasoning:
Both patches use the same core fix in `__asyncHydrate`'s `performHydrate`. They capture `wasConnected` up front, then bail if `!el.parentNode || (wasConnected && !el.isConnected)`. This addresses the root cause the issue identifies: a lazy strategy firing after the SSR node has been detached. It also keeps hydration working for apps that hydrate into a container never attached to the document. On correctness of the primary fix, the two are equivalent.

Patch A adds the defense-in-depth hardening the issue explicitly suggests. `getContainerType` now tolerates a `null` container, and the non-null assertion is dropped at the async-component call site. The change is minimal, type-correct and low-risk. It guards the other `parentNode(node)` call path, so the TypeError cannot resurface via a different route. A also documents the new guard with a comment explaining the intent.

On tests, B checks two cases with a detached root element and a detached ancestor. It asserts no throw and that the inner component never renders, which is a meaningful check that would fail before the fix.

A's tests are broader:
- a detached element root
- a detached fragment root, where `el` is the fragment anchor comment
- a detached ancestor, where the node keeps its parent but is disconnected
- a custom user-provided strategy, showing the guard is strategy-agnostic
- a positive control confirming a still-connected node does hydrate and gets its click listener

The positive control matters because it guards against a fix that simply never hydrates. B has no such check. A's assertions are also behavioral: the listener is not attached to the detached node.

With identical core logic, A wins on test thoroughness, including the regression guard against over-skipping, and on the issue-requested hardening. Neither adds risky scope.

issue_md:
### Vue version

3.5.33 

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://stackblitz.com/edit/vitejs-vite-ktsycrrc?file=repro.mjs

### Steps to reproduce

1. SSR-render an async component that uses hydrate: hydrateOnVisible().
2. On the client, hydration is deferred and the strategy registers an IntersectionObserver on the component's SSR node.
3. The node gets detached from the document before the observer's callback executes (in production this is a route change / re-render while the intersection callback is already queued).
4. The observer callback runs and invokes hydrate() against the now-detached node.

### What is expected?

A node that is no longer connected to the document should simply not be hydrated (there's nothing to hydrate), no exception thrown.

### What is actually happening?

hydrate() reaches hydrateNode, which computes the container type from the node's parent:

```
// packages/runtime-core/src/hydration.ts — inside hydrateNode, async-component branch
nextNode = vnode.type.hydrate(
  node, vnode, parentComponent, parentSuspense,
  getContainerType(parentNode(node)),   // parentNode(node) === null for a detached node
  slotScopeIds, optimized, rendererInternals, hydrateNode,
)
```

```
// packages/runtime-core/src/hydration.ts
const getContainerType = (container) => {
  if (container.nodeType !== 1) return undefined   // <-- container is null -> throws
  ...
}
```

For a detached node parentNode(node) is null, so getContainerType(null) throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'nodeType').

The async-component hydration wrapper only guards against the patched case, never against disconnection:

```
// packages/runtime-core/src/apiAsyncComponent.ts — __asyncHydrate
const performHydrate = () => {
  if (patched) { /* warn + */ return }   // only guards `patched`
  hydrate()                              // no isConnected check
}
```
Because the strategy runs inside load().then(...), the throw surfaces as an unhandledrejection, so app-level try/catch around the component can't catch it.

### System Info

```shell
vue: 3.5.33
@vue/server-renderer: 3.5.33
Environment where it triggers: Android WebView (Chrome), production SSR + client hydration
```

### Any additional comments?

We see this almost exclusively on Android Chrome WebView (~43k occurrences / ~12.8k users over a rollout window) on a page that lazy-hydrates several below-the-fold sections via hydrateOnVisible. The IntersectionObserver callback is dispatched asynchronously; when the user navigates/re-renders in the WebView, the observed node is detached between the intersection being recorded and the callback running, exactly the sequence above. Desktop rarely hits the race.

Skip hydration when the anchor node is no longer connected. the semantically correct place is the async performHydrate (or each built-in strategy's trigger), e.g. bail when no observed/anchor element isConnected:
 
```
const performHydrate = () => {
  if (patched) { return }
  if (el && !el.isConnected) return   // detached before hydration → nothing to hydrate
  hydrate()
}
```
As defense-in-depth, getContainerType could also tolerate a `null` container `(if (!container || container.nodeType !== 1) return undefined)`, since it's called with parentNode(node) at several sites.

We're currently shipping a userland wrapper around hydrateOnVisible that applies exactly the isConnected guard, which fully stops the crash.

title: defineModel: named model with PropType + factory default infers wrong generic (regression from #14968)

judge.reasoning: Correctness is the deciding factor. Patch B fixes the root cause. It adds dedicated overloads (both the unnamed and the named `defineModel` forms) where `type: PropType<T>` is the only inference site for `T`. Those overloads check `default` against `DefineModelDefault<NoInfer<T>>`, so a factory such as `() => []` can no longer become an inference candidate for `T`. That directly addresses the regression the issue describes. Vue's type surface already uses `NoInfer` elsewhere (e.g. `App.use`), so it adds no new TypeScript-version requirement. B's tests cover the reported case (named array with factory default), the unnamed form, object and primitive defaults, the explicit-generic path, and negative cases (wrong factory return type, raw array default, wrong primitive default). Patch A only swaps the order of the intersection members in the existing overloads. Any effect comes from TypeScript's candidate ordering and common-supertype selection, not from a structural guarantee. Even if A's added tests pass, the fix is fragile and could break with compiler changes or other option shapes. The main point against B is a large amount of unrelated churn: dozens of generated `.d.ts` files committed into `src` directories across compiler-core, reactivity, runtime-core and shared, many omitted for size. These are clutter and a maintenance risk (stale declarations next to sources), but they don't affect the logic of the fix, and `.ts` sources take precedence in resolution. My confidence is limited by not seeing the omitted files, though they appear to be the same kind of emitted declarations. On balance, B's sound, well-tested fix outweighs A's minimal but speculative reorder; B should drop the stray `.d.ts` files before merging.

issue_md:
### Vue version

3.5.39

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#

### Steps to reproduce

In the reproduction, `broken` declares a named model with a runtime `type: PropType<string[]>` plus a factory `default: () => []`. `fixed` declares the same thing but with the generic pinned explicitly (`defineModel<string[]>(...)`).

Run the type checker (or `vue-tsc --noEmit` locally) over this SFC.

### What is expected?

Both `broken` and `fixed` should type-check cleanly — this is the recommended pattern for avoiding shared mutable state (per #14966 / #14968): a factory default combined with a runtime `PropType` declaration.


### What is actually happening?

Only `broken` fails. TS infers the generic `T` from the `default` factory function's own type (`() => never[]`) instead of from the `type: PropType<string[]>` field:

error TS2769: No overload matches this call.
Overload 1 of 4, '(name: string, options: ({ required: true; } | { default: DefineModelDefault<() => never[]>; }) & Omit<PropOptions<() => never[], () => never[]>, "default"> & DefineModelOptions<...>): ModelRef<...>', gave the following error.
Type 'PropType<string[]>' is not assignable to type 'true | PropType<() => never[]> | null | undefined'.
Type 'new (...args: any[]) => string[]' is not assignable to type 'true | PropType<() => never[]> | null | undefined'.
Type 'new (...args: any[]) => string[]' is not assignable to type 'new (...args: any[]) => () => never[]'.
Type 'string[]' is not assignable to type '() => never[]'.
Type 'string[]' provides no match for the signature '(): never[]'.
Overload 2 of 4, '(name: string, options?: DefineModelRuntimeOptions<string[], string[], string[]> | undefined): ModelRef<string[] | undefined, string, string[] | undefined, string[] | undefined>', gave the following error.
Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'default' does not exist in type 'DefineModelRuntimeOptions<string[], string[], string[]>'.

his is a regression from #14968 (landed in 3.5.39), which introduced `DefineModelDefault<T> = InferDefault<Data, T>` for the named-model overload. When both a runtime `type: PropType<T>` field and a factory `default` are present on the same options object, TS resolves `T` from the `default` field first, breaking a pattern that worked prior to 3.5.39.

**Workaround:** explicitly pin the generic, as shown by `fixed` in the reproduction:

```ts
const fixed = defineModel<string[]>('visibility2', {
  type: Array as PropType<string[]>,
  default: () => [],
})
```

### System Info

```shell
vue: 3.5.39
vue-tsc: 3.3.7
typescript: 5.7.3
```

### Any additional comments?

Related to / regression from #14966 and #14968. Only reproduces on the **named** `defineModel(name, options)` overload when `type`/`PropType` and a factory `default` are combined; the unnamed `defineModel<T>({ ... })` form with an explicit generic is unaffected.

title: SSR memory leak - options API watchers are created and never stopped with async `setup()`

judge.reasoning:
The production code change is identical in both patches. Each wraps `handleSetupResult` in the async-setup `.then()` callback with `setInSSRSetupState(true)`, then resets it to false in a `finally`. This fixes the root cause: after the setup promise resolves, `finishComponentSetup`/`applyOptions` runs with `isInSSRComponentSetup` set, so `watch` options and `this.$watch` calls in `created()` follow SSR semantics. Non-immediate watchers become no-ops, and sync watchers are registered for SSR cleanup. Correctness is equal.

The difference is in the tests. Both include the issue's reproduction test, which fails before the fix and passes after. Patch A adds a GC/WeakRef retention test. It targets the memory-leak symptom directly, but it sits in a suite marked `describe.skipIf(!global.gc)`, so it only runs when GC is exposed. Patch B adds two always-run tests covering other paths through the same fix. One checks `this.$watch` inside `created()`, confirming non-immediate watchers stay inert while immediate ones run exactly once. The other checks a `flush: 'sync'` options watcher, which goes through the SSR cleanup-handle path rather than the NOOP path. These exercise distinct branches of the SSR watcher logic that the fix enables, so Patch B's regression coverage is broader and more reliably executed. Patch B also adds a short comment explaining why the SSR setup state is restored, which makes the intent clearer.

With code parity, Patch B's broader always-running tests and clearer comment make it the slightly better patch.

title: compileScript drops template imports from __returned__ when analysis re-runs on a transformed template AST

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the same way. When `ast.transformed` is set, `resolveTemplateAnalysisResult` re-parses the full SFC source in `parseMode: 'sfc'` with `prefixIdentifiers: true` and errors suppressed, then walks the fresh `<template>` children. Both thread `templateOptions` (compilerOptions such as delimiters) from `compileScript` into the analysis, for both the used-import check and the v-model demotion check. Correctness is essentially equivalent.

Patch A also extracts the re-parse into a shared `resolveTemplateAST` helper that `compileTemplate` now uses. That removes duplication and honours a custom `compiler`/`ssr`. However, it rewrites `compileTemplate`'s imports and logic, which is a modest extra risk. It also exports the internal `templateAnalysisCache` just so the test can clear it.

Patch B keeps the change local to `importUsageCheck.ts`, using compiler-dom's `parse`, which is the same parser the descriptor AST comes from.

On tests, Patch B is clearly stronger and maps directly onto the issue:
- It covers imports used in a template function call, in `v-for`, and as a component, and asserts unused imports stay excluded.
- It covers custom delimiters on re-parse.
- It covers recoverable parse errors not throwing.
- It covers v-model `SETUP_LET` demotion on a transformed AST.

Patch A has a single test, covering only a simple interpolation with custom delimiters, and it relies on reaching into the exported cache. Both test suites would fail before the fix. Patch B's coverage of the issue's specific scenarios (function-call expressions and v-for), together with its smaller blast radius, outweighs Patch A's deduplication.

title: Suspense: flushing buffered effects overflows the call stack when many effects accumulate while pending (RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded)

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the three spread-push sites the issue names: `queuePostFlushCb`, the nested `flushPostFlushCbs` merge into `activePostFlushCbs`, and the Suspense merge into a pending parent. Each replaces the spread with an indexed loop, so on those sites they are equivalent and correct.

Patch B also fixes a fourth site on the same buffering path that the issue does not list: `queueEffectWithSuspense` does `suspense.effects.push(...fn)` when `fn` is an array of lifecycle hooks. A large enough hook array would still overflow there under a pending suspense. This is low-risk hardening of the code that fills `suspense.effects`, and B tests it directly with a component registering 500k `onMounted` hooks.

On tests, A adds two scheduler unit tests with 1M-entry arrays. They cover `queuePostFlushCb` and the nested active-flush merge, and would fail before the fix. B adds equivalent scheduler tests. It also adds Suspense integration tests that reproduce the issue end to end: an async dependency plus a tree buffering 500k post effects, then flushing on resolve. One of these covers nested suspense, where the inner boundary resolves first and merges into the pending outer one. That exercises the `parent.effects` merge path, which A's tests never touch, so A's Suspense change is untested. B's tests are heavier to run but much closer to the reported scenario.

Craft is comparable: both use clear comments and simple loops consistent with the surrounding code. B wins on broader coverage of the overflow sites and more faithful regression tests.

### Vue version

3.5.39 (also reproduces on 3.5.40 / `@b5f8518` in the playground)

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open the playground and show the **Preview** pane.
2. The app renders a `<Suspense>` whose default slot contains an async component (resolves after ~4s) plus a large tree (2000 rows, each with a few `flush: 'post'` watchers).
3. While the suspense is pending, a timer keeps mutating a ref, so the still-mounted tree re-renders repeatedly. Each re-render buffers its post effects into `suspense.effects` (via `queueEffectWithSuspense`).
4. When the async component resolves, the suspense flushes the buffered effects.

### What is expected?

The buffered effects flush and the app keeps working.

### What is actually happening?

`Uncaught (in promise): RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` — thrown from `queuePostFlushCb` called by `suspense.resolve()`:

```text
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
    at queuePostFlushCb (runtime-core.esm-bundler.js:331)
    at Object.resolve   (runtime-core.esm-bundler.js:7426)
```

The scheduler dies mid-flush, leaving the app permanently wedged (blank page).

### Root cause

`suspense.effects` is unbounded — every post effect of every component under a pending suspense boundary is buffered into it. On resolve, the whole array is flushed with a spread call:

- `scheduler.ts`: `pendingPostFlushCbs.push(...cb)`
- `scheduler.ts` (`flushPostFlushCbs` nested case): `activePostFlushCbs.push(...deduped)`
- `Suspense.ts` (merge into pending parent): `parent.effects.push(...effects)`

Spreading an array into a function call is limited by the engine's call stack (~100k–200k args in V8), so once enough effects accumulate the flush itself throws.

### Real-world impact

We hit this in production in a Nuxt app: a kanban board page with ~1000 mounted cards that re-renders once per second (elapsed-time ticker). Navigating to another page keeps the board mounted under `<NuxtPage>`'s pending Suspense; its buffered effects exceed the spread limit and every SPA navigation away from the board crashes with a permanent white screen (hard reload of the target URL works fine, since there is no pending suspense in that case).

### Suggested fix

Replace the unbounded spread pushes with plain loops. I have a PR ready with the fix and a regression test (queuePostFlushCb with a 1M-entry array).

title: Custom elements: async components nested ≥3 levels crash with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'provides')` — chained child resolve races its parent's mount

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the same core fix. The chain callback now returns `this._resolveDef()`, and `_resolveDef()` returns the parent's own `_pendingResolve` (the asyncDef().then(resolve) promise). As a result, a chained parent's `_pendingResolve` settles only after that parent's async load finishes and it mounts. This restores ancestor-first mounting at any depth, which is the issue's first suggested direction and the root cause.

The patches differ in the extra edge they cover.

Patch A also handles an already-resolved element (`_resolved` true, `_instance` null) that is re-connected under a still-pending async parent. The original code calls `_mount` immediately in that case, so `_inheritParentContext` would hit the same `parent._instance === null` dereference. That is the same class of crash the issue describes, so A closes a second path to it. Its tests cover:
- 3 levels with the slowest middle level (the issue's exact scenario).
- 4 levels with descending load times (the cascade case).
- The re-connect case.
All three check mount order, shadow DOM content and the full provide/inject chain at each level. They would fail before the fix.

Patch B adds an `isConnected` guard so a child detached while waiting does not resolve. That is reasonable but tangential, and does not address a crash path. B's main test is deterministic and well built, with explicit resolvers and inject checks, but it covers only depth 3. Its second test exercises B's own tangential guard.

A's tests rely on real timeouts, which is slightly less deterministic, but the margins are generous. Overall, A fixes the root cause equally well, covers an additional crash path the issue implies, and tests deeper nesting, so A is the better fix.

title: The Playground's TS version is set to 7 by default.

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the same way: they pass a `typescriptVersion` ref into `useStore` so the playground no longer defaults to @vue/repl's 'latest', which now resolves to TS 7.

Patch A hardcodes the exact version '6.0.3'. It works today, but it will go stale as new 6.x patch releases ship, and someone has to remember to bump it. It adds no tests and does not explain why the pin exists.

Patch B defaults to the major range '6', which the CDN resolves to the newest stable 6.x release, so it keeps tracking TS 6 updates without maintenance. It also handles a consequence of using a range: the version dropdown would otherwise highlight no entry. The new `isActiveVersion` helper in VersionSelect.vue resolves '6' to the newest non-prerelease 6.x entry. It also keeps the existing 'latest' and exact-match behaviour. A comment explains why TS 7 is avoided.

Patch B adds a spec. It checks that the default is '6' and resolves to 6.0.3, not 7.0.0 or a 6.1 beta, and it covers the highlighting cases. The test on the default value would fail before the change.

The small risk in B is that @vue/repl internals might not handle a range string as well as an exact version, but CDN URLs accept major ranges. The added module is small and focused. On balance, B is the more durable and better-tested fix.

title: KeepAlive caches a never-mounted vnode when a switch lands while an ancestor Suspense is pending

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the same source change in KeepAlive.ts. Inside the post-render effect queued on the Suspense, each one skips `cache.set` when the inner child has no `component`. This matches the issue's root-cause analysis and the existing 'avoid caching vnode that not been mounted' guards, so on correctness they are equivalent. They differ in their tests. Patch B's test reproduces the issue's tree exactly: an outer Suspense whose Fragment holds an async RootDep and a KeepAlive wrapping an inner Suspense, with a keyed component. It switches pages while the ancestor is pending, lets the ancestor resolve, then switches A→B→A. Without the guard, the poisoned PageB cache entry would hit the null `component` path on the later switches, so the test fails before the fix and passes after. It uses only the spec file's known `defineAsyncComponent(comp, delay)` helper and the `deps` array, and it explains why the post-resolve state is matched with a regex: the skipped patch is not replayed on resolve. Patch A's test calls `defineAsyncComp`, which does not appear in the diff and may not exist in the spec file. It also mixes an external promise for RootDep with timing tricks (`setTimeout`, multiple awaits) and hard-codes the post-resolve page as A. That makes it more fragile and possibly unrunnable. Patch B also adds a short comment explaining why the inner child can be unmounted, which helps future readers. With identical fixes, B's clearer and more self-contained test gives it the edge.

issue_md:
### Vue version

3.5.41 (also reproduces on 3.5.40 and 3.6.0-rc.3)

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#

### Steps to reproduce

The reproduction drives itself from `onMounted` — just open it and read the log. The tree is the one Nuxt renders for a page with `<NuxtPage keepalive>`:

```
<Suspense>            <!-- root boundary, still pending -->
  <RootDep />         <!-- async setup, resolves after 300ms -->
  <KeepAlive>
    <Suspense>        <!-- per-page boundary -->
      <component :is="page" :key="key" />
    </Suspense>
  </KeepAlive>
</Suspense>
```

1. While `RootDep` is still pending (so `parentSuspense.deps > 0`), switch the inner page from `PageA` to `PageB`.
2. Let the root boundary resolve.
3. Switch back to `PageA`, then to `PageB` again.

### What is expected?

The inner page follows the switches, and no errors are raised.

### What is actually happening?

The rendered page is stuck on `PageA` forever — every later switch is a no-op — and the renderer throws:

```
Cannot read properties of null (reading 'suspenseId')   // patchSuspense
Cannot read properties of null (reading 'm')            // unmountComponent
```

In a production build the second one is the more familiar
`Uncaught (in promise) TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'bum' of 'instance' as it is null.`

Removing the `<KeepAlive>` and changing nothing else makes both errors go away and navigation work.

### System Info

```shell
  System:
    OS: Linux 7.0 Ubuntu 26.04 LTS
    CPU: (4) x64 Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-8700 CPU @ 3.20GHz
    Memory: 5.86 GB / 11.67 GB
  Binaries:
    Node: 24.19.0
    npm: 11.19.0
  npmPackages:
    vue: 3.5.41
  Browsers:
    Chromium (Playwright 1.5x, headless)
```

### Any additional comments?

**The chain**, as far as I could trace it:

1. The route change re-renders `KeepAlive`, so the inner `<Suspense>` is patched with `n1 != null`. Because an **ancestor** boundary is still pending, `SuspenseImpl.process` takes its early return:

   ```js
   if (parentSuspense && parentSuspense.deps > 0 && !n1.suspense.isInFallback) {
     n2.suspense = n1.suspense
     n2.suspense.vnode = n2
     n2.el = n1.el
     return
   }
   ```

   The incoming page vnode is therefore never patched: `vnode.component === null`, `vnode.el === null`.

2. `KeepAlive`'s `onUpdated` → `cacheSubtree` still caches it, unconditionally:

   ```js
   if (isSuspense(instance.subTree.type)) {
     queuePostRenderEffect(() => {
       cache.set(pendingCacheKey, getInnerChild(instance.subTree))
     }, instance.subTree.suspense)
   }
   ```

3. The next render for that key hits the poisoned entry: `KeepAlive` copies `cachedVNode.component` (`null`) onto the new vnode and sets `COMPONENT_KEPT_ALIVE`, so `patchSuspense` reads `newBranch.component.suspenseId` on `null`, and the teardown that follows calls `unmountComponent(null)`.

**Suggested fix** — the same shape as the two guards already at that site, i.e. do not cache a vnode that never finished mounting:

```js
const innerChild = getInnerChild(instance.subTree)
if (innerChild.component) {
  cache.set(pendingCacheKey, innerChild)
}
```

With that guard the page is simply not cached that one time, and the reproduction runs clean.

This looks like a third path into the defect class fixed by #10912 (`avoid caching vnode that not been mounted`, for #10899) and #11479 (for #6028) — both guard `KeepAlive`'s **own** subtree, while here it is an **ancestor** `Suspense` that is pending.

Real-world context: this is how it surfaced for us — a Nuxt 4 app rendering `<NuxtPage :keepalive="{ max: 5 }" />`, where a link clicked before hydration finished intermittently left the user on a blank page with `Cannot destructure property 'bum' of 'e' as it is null` in the console. The window widens with slower hydration, so it shows up under load / on slow clients.

<sub>Investigation and reproduction prepared with Claude Code, on behalf of drunomics.</sub>

title: looseEqual() reports Map and Set instances with different contents as equal

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause correctly. Each adds explicit Map/Set branches to `looseEqual`, rejects mismatched types (Map vs Set, Map vs object, Set vs array), checks size first, and does order-insensitive loose matching where each element pairs with a distinct counterpart.

Patch B handles both collection types with one helper, `looseCompareCollections`. Iterating a Map yields `[k, v]` tuples, which `looseEqual` compares as arrays, so keys and values are compared loosely. Its branches sit inside the `isObject` block, which is also correct.

Patch A has separate Map and Set comparators. Each has a SameValueZero fast path that falls back to the same unordered loose matching. I traced the fast paths and found no cases where they diverge from the fallback:
- A Set whose members all pass `has()` with equal size is genuinely equal.
- A Map with shared keys and loosely equal values would also pass the fallback.

The fast paths add code but no correctness risk, and they make the common case cheaper.

The main difference is tests, which rank above craft.
- **Patch A** tests: empty vs non-empty in both directions, key-order insensitivity, loose values and loose object keys, the distinct-match requirement, nested Sets/Maps inside objects and arrays, and cross-type cases. It also extends the `v-model` select test to Sets, reactive updates and the no-match (-1) case, and adds SSR `ssrRenderDynamicModel` assertions.
- **Patch B** tests: the core cases plus one static `v-model` select assertion for Maps only.

Patch B is more concise and arguably cleaner. However, Patch A's broader, meaningful coverage of the issue's scenarios outweighs B's smaller craft advantage.

### Steps to reproduce

`looseEqual()` in `packages/shared/src/looseEqual.ts` reports unrelated `Map` and `Set` instances as equal:

```ts
import { looseEqual } from '@vue/shared'

looseEqual(new Map([['a', 1]]), new Map([['b', 2]])) // true, expected false
looseEqual(new Set([1]), new Set([2]))               // true, expected false
looseEqual(new Map([['a', 1]]), new Map())           // true, expected false
```

This surfaces to users through `v-model` on `<select>`. The following selects the **wrong** option:

```ts
const mapA = new Map([['id', 1]])
const mapB = new Map([['id', 2]])
const selected = ref(mapB)
```

```vue
<select v-model="selected">
  <option :value="mapA">A</option>
  <option :value="mapB">B</option>
</select>
```

`el.selectedIndex` is `0` (option A) when it should be `1`, because `looseEqual(mapA, mapB)` returns `true` and the loop in `setSelected` stops at the first option.

### What is expected?

`Map`/`Set` values with different contents compare as not equal, so `v-model` selects the option that actually matches.

### What is actually happening?

`Map` and `Set` fall through to the generic object branch. `Object.keys()` on either is always `[]`, so the key-count check passes and the `for...in` loop body never executes — entries are never compared. Execution then reaches the final line:

```ts
return String(a) === String(b)
```

Every `Map` stringifies to `'[object Map]'` and every `Set` to `'[object Set]'`, so any two of the same type are reported equal.

Note this differs from `Date` and `Symbol`, which are given explicit branches above, and from arrays and plain objects, which compare correctly:

```ts
looseEqual([1], [2])       // false, correct
looseEqual({ a: 1 }, { a: 2 }) // false, correct
```

`packages/shared/__tests__/looseEqual.spec.ts` has 13 cases but none for `Map`/`Set`, which is why this hasn't been caught.

### Possible fix

Add explicit branches before the generic object check, mirroring the existing `Date`/`Symbol` pattern. `isMap` and `isSet` already exist in `packages/shared/src/general.ts`. `Set` needs content comparison rather than reference lookup to stay consistent with `looseEqual`'s semantics (e.g. `new Set([{ a: 1 }])` vs `new Set([{ a: 1 }])`).

Worth confirming the intended semantics first: should `Map` comparison be key-order-insensitive, and should `Set` compare loosely (`looseEqual` per element) or strictly? Happy to open a PR with tests once the direction is confirmed.

### System Info

```
Vue: 3.5.x / main @ a2b40db
```

### Any additional comments?

Unrelated to #15298, which touches only `vModel.ts`.

title: Suspense `timeout` + Transition `out-in`: parent update during the fallback swap permanently drops the resolved branch

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the same core fix in `patchSuspense`. They skip `patch(activeBranch, newFallback)` and `setActiveBranch` while `suspense.isFallbackMountPending` is true, in both the `isInFallback` paths. They also change the deferred `mountFallback` to mount the latest `suspense.vnode.ssFallback`, so a fallback update skipped during the window is not lost. This targets the root cause described in the issue: `activeBranch` is no longer hijacked by the fallback, and `resolve()` hooks onto the leaving content's real afterLeave.

The only code difference is small. A uses the latest `ssFallback` only when `delayEnter` is true and otherwise keeps the passed `fallbackVNode`. B always uses `ssFallback`. In the immediate path these should be the same vnode, because `suspense.vnode` is already updated before `fallback(newFallback)` is called. So B's version is probably equivalent, but A's is the more conservative change and leaves the non-deferred behavior exactly as before.

Tests are where they differ most. A adds deterministic unit tests in Suspense.spec using `BaseTransition` with manually held `onLeave` done callbacks, as the issue's event-ordered repro does. They cover three orderings:
- Resolve before leave completes: the exact bug.
- Leave completes before resolve, which also checks the latest fallback is mounted and stays reactive.
- Switching to a second async branch while the mount is pending.

A's tests also assert that the fallback is not mounted early after the parent update. B adds e2e tests that rely on wall-clock timeouts, a 10ms Suspense timeout plus buffer, and `transitionFinish` durations. They are more timing-sensitive and cover fewer orderings, though they do reproduce the real-world scenario and check the latest-fallback behavior.

B's comments explain the failure mode a bit more thoroughly, but the craft is otherwise comparable. With the fixes essentially equal, A wins on more precise, deterministic and broader test coverage and a slightly more conservative change.

issue_md:
### Version
3.5.41

### Reproduction link
[play.vuejs.org/](https://play.vuejs.org/#)

### Steps to reproduce
Open the playground with Vue **3.5.41** selected (the banner in the preview shows the actually running version). The repro is fully event-ordered (JS transition hooks hold the leave open), so it fails on the first run, every run:

1. A keyed component inside `<Suspense :timeout="100">` inside `<Transition mode="out-in">` navigates to a cold async component (`defineAsyncComponent`, chunk not loaded yet).
2. `timeout` elapses → Suspense starts the fallback swap; the old content's leave transition begins.
3. While the leave is in progress, the parent re-renders (in a real app: a ResizeObserver callback, a store update — anything).
4. The async component resolves; the leave finishes.

### What is expected?
The resolved page is mounted (with the fallback shown in between).

### What is actually happening?
`@resolve` fires and the module is loaded, but the page is never inserted — the fallback stays on screen forever. No error, no warning. A later unrelated parent re-render "un-sticks" it, which is why this is so hard to catch in the wild.

Removing any one of the three ingredients — the `timeout`, `mode="out-in"`, or the mid-swap parent re-render — makes it pass (all three controls verified).

The bug is deterministic: 3.5.30 passes, 3.5.31+ fails (bisected).

---

**Root cause (bisected + traced)**

Regression introduced by 908c6ad05 (#9392, first released in 3.5.31), which added `isFallbackMountPending`:

- `fallback()` sets `isFallbackMountPending = true` and defers `mountFallback` to the leaving branch's `afterLeave`.
- A parent re-render hits `patchSuspense`'s `isInFallback` path, which patches `activeBranch` → `newFallback` and calls `setActiveBranch(suspense, newFallback)` — mounting the fallback early without clearing `isFallbackMountPending`.
- `resolve()` then skips `unmount(activeBranch)` because the flag is still true, yet hooks the content move onto `activeBranch.transition.afterLeave` — where `activeBranch` is now the fallback, which is never unmounted. The `afterLeave` never fires; the resolved branch is lost.

Before #9392, `resolve()` unconditionally unmounted the active branch, so the fallback left and its `afterLeave` inserted the content.

A guard in `patchSuspense` fixes it — while `isFallbackMountPending` is true, `activeBranch` is still the leaving content, so the `patch(activeBranch, newFallback)` + `setActiveBranch(suspense, newFallback)` calls in the `isInFallback` paths must be skipped. Happy to submit a PR with the fix and an e2e regression test (prepared and passing locally, including the #9392 test for #7966).

Real-world impact: in our production SPA (layout = `RouterView` → `Transition out-in` → `Suspense timeout`, per the documented pattern) roughly 1 in 10 cold first navigations ended on an infinite spinner — console clean, all network requests succeed.

title: [compiler-sfc] Typo 'exit' instead of 'leave' in estree-walker causes missing ASI guard and runtime error with consecutive awaits

judge.reasoning:
Both patches make the same source fix: they rename `exit` to `leave` in the estree-walker options. This addresses the root cause. `scope.pop()` now runs when leaving a BlockStatement, so the `needsSemi` lookup checks the correct enclosing block's statement list. On correctness the two are identical.

The difference is in the tests. Both sets would fail before the fix and pass after it.

Patch A adds two cases built on the existing `assertAwaitDetection` helper and snapshot convention used throughout this describe block. The cases are a nested `if` inside an `if`, and a `while` inside a `try`. Each asserts with regexes that a `;(` ASI guard precedes both the first await (right after the closing `}` of the nested block) and the second await. These assertions target exactly the guard the issue says is missing. Covering two block shapes (if/if and try/while) gives somewhat broader evidence that the scope stack is now balanced. The snapshot entries are consistent with the assertions.

Patch B adds one test that compiles the SFC, strips the import, evaluates the output with `new Function` and a stubbed `_withAsyncContext`, and checks that `setup` resolves. This reproduces the runtime TypeError symptom directly, which is a nice touch. However, it relies on an ad-hoc eval harness and regex stripping of the import line, and that departs from the file's established pattern. It also covers only one scenario.

Scope is equally minimal in both patches. On tests and craft, A fits the surrounding conventions better and covers more cases, so A is slightly better.
