### Vue version

3.5.40

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://play.vuejs.org/#

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open the SFC Playground link.
2. Click on the **"JS"** tab in the right panel to view the compiled output.
3. Observe the compiled code for the two `await` statements.
4. Notice that there is no semicolon (`;`) inserted between the two `_withAsyncContext` blocks.

### What is expected?

1. Open the SFC Playground link.
2. Click on the **"JS"** tab in the right panel to view the compiled output.
3. Observe the compiled code for the two `await` statements.
4. Notice that there is no semicolon (`;`) inserted between the two `_withAsyncContext` blocks.

### What is actually happening?

### **What is actually happening? ***
```markdown
The ASI guard (`;`) is missing. 

Because of this, the JavaScript engine interprets the second statement as a function call invoked on the result of the first statement, causing a runtime error: `TypeError: (...) is not a function`.

```javascript
  ([__temp,__restore] = _withAsyncContext(() => Promise.resolve(1))),
  await __temp,
  __restore()
)( // <--- RUNTIME ERROR
  ([__temp,__restore] = _withAsyncContext(() => Promise.resolve(2))),
  await __temp,
  __restore()
)
```

### System Info

```shell
System:
    OS: Linux 5.10 Debian GNU/Linux 11 (bullseye) 11 (bullseye)
    CPU: (4) x64 AMD EPYC 9575F 64-Core Processor
    Memory: 6.69 GB / 11.65 GB
    Container: Yes
    Shell: 5.1.4 - /bin/bash
  Binaries:
    Node: 24.14.1 - /root/.nvm/versions/node/v24.14.1/bin/node
    Yarn: 1.22.22 - /root/.yarn/bin/yarn
    npm: 11.11.0 - /root/.nvm/versions/node/v24.14.1/bin/npm
    pnpm: 10.33.0 - /root/.nvm/versions/node/v24.14.1/bin/pnpm
  Browsers:
    Chrome: 150.0.7871.181
  npmPackages:
    vue: ^3.5.40 => 3.5.40
```

### Any additional comments?

**Root Cause:**
The bug is caused by a typo in the AST walker configuration inside `compiler-sfc`. The compiler uses `estree-walker` which expects the hooks `{ enter, leave }`. However, the code currently passes `{ enter, exit }`.

Since `exit` is not a valid hook in `estree-walker`, it is never called. Consequently, `scope.pop()` is never executed when leaving a `BlockStatement` (like the `if` block in the reproduction). This corrupts the `scope` stack, causing the `needsSemi` calculation to fail for all subsequent `AwaitExpression` nodes.

**Proposed Fix:**
Simply change `exit` to `leave` in the walker options:

```diff
-  exit(node2) {
+  leave(node2) {
     if (node2.type === "BlockStatement") scope.pop();
   }

title: compiler-sfc: loadTSConfig re-parses the whole tsconfig extends chain for every config it walks

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the same way: a module-level `Map<string, TS.ExtendedConfigCacheEntry>` passed as the 8th argument of `parseJsonConfigFileContent`. The cache itself is equivalent in both, and both clear it wholesale on invalidation, which is correct because cached entries embed their own extends chains. They differ in how invalidation answers the issue's dev/HMR caveat.

Patch A clears the extended cache only when a `.json` file is invalidated, and also clears `tsConfigCache` in that case. This matters because `tsConfigCache` is keyed by the top-level config path. If only `tsconfig.base.json` changes, a dev server invalidates just that file. Under Patch B, the parsed configs that extend it would stay stale in `tsConfigCache` even though the extended cache was cleared. Patch A therefore makes an edited shared base actually take effect end-to-end.

Patch B calls `tsConfigExtendedCache.clear()` on every `invalidateTypeCache` call, including ordinary `.vue`/`.ts` edits. During dev this wipes the cache on almost every HMR update, which undercuts the performance gain the issue is about. B's own invalidation test has to manually invalidate `/tsconfig.json` as well as the base to pass, which exposes this gap rather than covering it.

On tests, Patch B is stronger. It checks base reads both within one traversal and across separate top-level lookups, and it adds an edit-after-invalidation test. Patch A has a single read-counting test that would fail before the change and pass after, with no invalidation test.

Overall, Patch A's more targeted and more complete invalidation outweighs B's broader test coverage.

issue_md:
### Vue version

3.5.42 (latest release; also present on `main` at 5409708)

### Link to minimal reproduction

https://github.com/cainrus/vue-compiler-sfc-tsconfig-repro

### Steps to reproduce

```sh
git clone https://github.com/cainrus/vue-compiler-sfc-tsconfig-repro
cd vue-compiler-sfc-tsconfig-repro
npm install
npm run repro
```

The generator builds a workspace of 150 packages, each with its own `tsconfig.json` that
`extends` one shared base and declares `references` to its group, plus one SFC per package whose
props type is imported from another package by alias. Both arms compile the same components; the
`cached` arm differs only in that it supplies an `extendedConfigCache`, through the public
`registerTS` hook, as the 8th argument the package leaves undefined.

### What is expected?

Parsing the same `extends` chain repeatedly should reuse the parsed parent configs, as TypeScript's
own `extendedConfigCache` parameter exists to allow.

### What is actually happening?

`loadTSConfig` calls `ts.parseJsonConfigFileContent` with five arguments, so the 8th
(`extendedConfigCache`) is always `undefined`:

https://github.com/vuejs/core/blob/main/packages/compiler-sfc/src/script/resolveType.ts

```js
const config = ts.parseJsonConfigFileContent(
  ts.readConfigFile(configPath, fs.readFile).config,
  parseConfigHost,           // 2
  dirname(configPath),       // 3
  undefined,                 // 4
  configPath,                // 5
)                            // 6, 7, 8 omitted -- the 8th is extendedConfigCache
```

and then recurses through project references:

```js
res.unshift(...loadTSConfig(refPath, ts, fs, visited))
```

So in a workspace whose packages all extend a shared base, that base is re-read and re-parsed once
per config the traversal reaches, and **each parse allocates its own fully expanded `paths` map**.
`visited` is a default parameter: it de-duplicates within one top-level call, never across calls.

Measured on the reproduction — node 22.23.2, `@vue/compiler-sfc` 3.5.41, `typescript` 5.9, one arm
per process (`tsConfigCache` is module scope):

| arm | config parses | distinct expanded `paths` objects | time | retained heap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| stock | 2900 | **2900** | 11.1 s | **1346.8 MB** |
| cached | 2900 | **1** | 1.9 s | **30.2 MB** |

The parse count is identical in both arms. The cache does not remove parses — it makes each one
cheap and stops the expanded options object from being rebuilt. Retained heap is `heapUsed` after a
forced GC.

On a production Vue monorepo (2432 components, 514 tsconfigs, 4051 project references, a 118 KB
shared base with 1342 `paths` entries), compiling 400 of its real components through
`compileScript` with the same two arms:

| arm | config parses | distinct expanded `paths` objects | time | retained heap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| stock | 7351 | **7350** | 25.4 s | **2615.8 MB** |
| cached | 7351 | **3** | 8.0 s | **188.7 MB** |

That is what led to this report: tsconfig parsing dominated the allocation profile of that
application's production build.

### Does the cache change the result?

`node parity.mjs` in the reproduction re-implements `loadTSConfig` verbatim and runs it twice per
entry config, differing only in the 8th argument, comparing resolved `compilerOptions`,
`projectReferences` and `fileNames` for every parse the traversal produces:

| run | parses compared | `paths` entries compared | mismatches |
|---|---|---|---|
| `node parity.mjs` | 400 | 176 000 | **0** |
| `MUTATE=1 node parity.mjs` (cached arm reads a different config) | 400 | 176 000 | 336 |
| `MUTATE=2 node parity.mjs` (one `paths` entry altered after parsing) | 400 | 176 000 | 400 |

The two controls are there because a comparator that always prints zero proves nothing. The same
comparison over the production monorepo's configs: 831 parses, 1 116 033 `paths` entries, 0
mismatches, with the controls reporting 114 and 831.

One consequence worth stating explicitly: with the cache, the expanded options object is **shared
by reference** (that is where the memory saving comes from), so it must not be handed to a consumer
that mutates it. `resolveWithTS` only reads `matchedConfig.config.options`, so that holds today.

### Suggested fix

A module-level `Map` threaded into the 8th argument. One caveat a fix has to answer:
`invalidateTypeCache` currently clears `tsConfigCache` and `tsConfigRefMap`, and would need to clear
the new cache too, or an edited `tsconfig.base.json` would go stale in dev/HMR — TypeScript keys
`extendedConfigCache` by resolved path, so that is a targeted delete.

PR: #15480 — it also explains why a plain `Map` rather than `createCache()`, and why
`invalidateTypeCache` clears the cache instead of deleting one entry.

### System Info

```
node 22.23.2, darwin arm64
@vue/compiler-sfc 3.5.41
typescript 5.9
```

### Any additional comments?

There is a second, independent problem in the same function's caller — `tsConfigCache` is an LRU
capped at 500 — which I am filing separately, since the fix for it is a capacity decision rather
than a one-line change.

title: [compiler-sfc] Top-level await inside switch case generates invalid code (missing semicolon before rewrite)

judge.reasoning: The source changes are functionally identical. Both push `SwitchCase.consequent` onto the scope stack on enter and pop it on leave. That makes the `needsSemi` check see sibling statements inside a case branch, which is the root cause named in the issue. The only source difference is brace style in `leave`, which doesn't matter. The deciding factor is the tests. Patch A compiles the SFC, actually runs `setup()` with a stubbed `_withAsyncContext`, and checks execution order through a `calls` array. That proves the generated code behaves correctly at runtime, not just that a `;` appears in the output. Patch A also covers the variants the issue lists: an await after an expression statement in a case, consecutive awaits in one case (the `(...)(...)` problem the issue calls out), an await as the first statement of a case (should get no prefix), and a root-level await after a switch (checks the scope stack is popped correctly). Each of these would fail or misbehave before the fix. Patch B adds two snapshot tests with a regex for `;(`, covering the basic case and the nested-in-`if` case from the issue. They are valid regression tests but only check the text shape. They skip the consecutive-awaits variant and the scope-restoration edge cases, and they add snapshot churn. With equal correctness, Patch A's broader, behavior-level tests make it the better patch.

[compiler-sfc] Top-level await inside `switch` case generates invalid code (missing semicolon before rewrite)

### Vue version
3.5.42 — also reproduced on `main` (5409708)

### Link to minimal reproduction
https://play.vuejs.org/#N4IgbgpgTgzglgewHYgFwgMwDoCsWAsATCADQgBmcANhDGqDFAMYD0AggA4dZgCuE9EE2QAXCEhFoQAHjEBbDlQCGYgHwAdJAAIt0gCZwwqqBA5QE0lgaObL8xSogaktmEyhwOIrTAgjeHM5wCghQ3sBaJuRaAL5a5OZyWgDkfBDJmprCSDDeSloAvJEQ5AAUIlD8AJRZyLlaAEaFxWUAjDUuSOS8SEwiiNoAjrwAHqVVWsCaOiwsxf5QOVo9eiVwSBB6WshaHLxQHAi+mjGZSEowAJ698T19A41KUOOT0-P72kQnZ3DRpUo8JRUaqvbQ+ADucBETAAFlpSg1AcCIBMpmCdEwLhAtK1UG8dDphmMOgSCUpwUooY9niTYt8kJY3B4vM5SCA4DA2PdIGgKvwYmRGKw5JSkFgRHRUKBsmIJFJgocwpMtO4II5OBxYvFEik0hkkArQt4NdqEElklh2FwePx9VkTOquKUNVUsHIED0RKVkgBiJRcZIdNkcrn9HmoPkQGICkAILwDSXAaNAA

### Steps to reproduce
1. Open the playground link above (or compile the SFC below with `@vue/compiler-sfc`).
2. The component `setup()` throws `TypeError: object is not iterable (cannot read property Symbol(Symbol.iterator))`.

SFC:

```vue
<script setup>
const a = true
const b = 1
function qux() {}
async function bar() { return 42 }
if (a) {
  switch (b) {
    case 1:
      qux()
      await bar()
  }
}
</script>
```

### What is expected?
The compiled `setup()` should run fine: `qux()` and `await bar()` should be two independent statements.

### What is actually happening?
The top-level `await` rewrite in `compileScript` emits the `withAsyncContext` wrapper expression **without a leading semicolon** when the `await` is inside a `switch` case that is not the first statement:

```js
async setup(__props, { expose: __expose }) {
  ...
  if (a) {
    switch (b) {
      case 1:
        qux()
        (
  ([__temp,__restore] = _withAsyncContext(() => bar())),
  await __temp,
  __restore()
)
    }
  }
}
```

Because the next line starts with `(`, ASI does not insert a semicolon, so the two lines are parsed as a single call expression `qux()(...)`. `bar()` is never awaited in the intended way and the runtime throws `TypeError: object is not iterable`.

The same code inside a plain block (not a `switch`) is compiled correctly with a leading `;`:

```js
if (a) {
  qux()
  ;(
  ([__temp,__restore] = _withAsyncContext(() => bar())),
  await __temp,
  __restore()
)
}
```

### Additional comments
Root cause: in `packages/compiler-sfc/src/compileScript.ts`, the scope stack used to decide whether the rewrite needs a semicolon only pushes/pops on `BlockStatement`. A `switch` statement's `SwitchCase.consequent` statement list is not tracked, so `needsSemi` is misjudged as `false` for `await` expressions inside case branches (unless the await happens to be the very first statement of the case).

Related variants also affected:
- Two consecutive top-level awaits inside one case produce `(...)(...)` back-to-back (second one also parsed as a call of the first result).
- Any `await` that follows an expression statement inside a case branch.

No prior issue found for this.

title: looseEqual: comparing Map/Set values with circular references throws RangeError (regression in 3.5.42)

judge.reasoning:
Both patches stop the unbounded recursion by threading a per-call 'seen' state through arrays, objects, Maps and Sets. Both handle the issue's three repro shapes: mutually-referencing Set elements, Map values with peers, and self-containing Sets. Both also fix the plain-object cycle case.

Correctness: Patch A tracks (a, b) pairs currently on the recursion stack and returns true when a pair is met again. This is exactly the approach the issue suggests, and it gives coinductive structural equality. A wraps the comparison in try/finally so the state is always cleaned up, and it keeps the public `looseEqual(a, b)` signature unchanged by adding an internal `looseEqualImpl`.

Patch B enforces a bijection between visited nodes. That is also cycle-safe, and it deliberately treats a self-loop and a 2-cycle as unequal (a stricter semantics than the issue asks for, but defensible). However, B adds an optional third `seen` parameter to the exported `looseEqual`. This leaks an internal detail into the public API. It is also risky: any caller that passes `looseEqual` directly as a callback which supplies a third argument would hand it a bogus state tuple. B also has no try/finally, though that matters little because the state is per call.

Tests: A adds unit tests for Sets, Maps (including self-reference), and cyclic objects and arrays. It also adds a runtime-dom `vModel` test that reproduces the issue's actual scenario (`<select v-model>` with cyclic Set and Map option values) and checks that the correct option is selected. B only adds shared unit tests, including a reasonable symmetry test, but has no component-level coverage of the reported failure.

Scope and craft: Both are comparably scoped. A's change is a cleaner wrapper around the existing logic. B moves the object, Map and Set logic into a new helper and introduces a callback indirection (`looseCompareNested`), which is somewhat harder to follow.

Overall A is the better fix: it follows the issue's suggested semantics, keeps the API clean, and tests the reported scenario end-to-end.

### Vue version
3.5.42 (also reproduced on current `main`, commit `5409708`)

### Link to minimal reproduction
https://play.vuejs.org/#eyJBcHAudnVlIjogIjxzY3JpcHQgc2V0dXA-XG5pbXBvcnQgeyByZWYgfSBmcm9tICd2dWUnXG5cbmNvbnN0IG1ha2VHcmFwaCA9ICgpID0--XG4gIDxzZWxlY3Qgdi1tb2RlbD1cInNlbGVjdGVkXCI-XG4gICAgPG9wdGlvbiA6dmFsdWU9XCJvcHRBXCI-QTwvb3B0aW9uPlxuICAgIDxvcHRpb24gOnZhbHVlPVwib3B0QlwiPkI8L29wdGlvbj5cbiAgPC9zZWxlY3Q-XG48L3RlbXBsYXRlPlxuIiwgImltcG9ydC1tYXAuanNvbiI6ICJ7XCJpbXBvcnRzXCI6IHtcInZ1ZVwiOiBcImh0dHBzOi8vdW5wa2cuY29tL0B2dWUvcnVudGltZS1kb21AMy41LjQyL2Rpc3QvcnVudGltZS1kb20uZXNtLWJyb3dzZXIuanNcIn19In0=

### Steps to reproduce
Open the reproduction above: a `<select v-model>` whose option `:value`s are `Set`s containing mutually-referencing objects. The component throws during mount, before any interaction.

```vue
<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const makeGraph = () => {
  const n1 = { id: 1 }
  const n2 = { id: 2 }
  n1.peer = n2
  n2.peer = n1  // circular reference
  return new Set([n1, n2])
}

const optA = makeGraph()
const optB = makeGraph()
const selected = ref(optB)
</script>

<template>
  <select v-model="selected">
    <option :value="optA">A</option>
    <option :value="optB">B</option>
  </select>
</template>
```

### What is expected?
Mounting the select should not throw. `looseEqual` should safely terminate on cyclic structures (e.g. by tracking already-visited pairs) and return `true` for two structurally identical cyclic Sets/Maps.

### What is actually happening?
Mounting throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`:

```
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
    at looseCompareCollections (packages/shared/src/looseEqual.ts:16)
    at looseEqual (packages/shared/src/looseEqual.ts:64)
    at looseCompareCollections (packages/shared/src/looseEqual.ts:22)
    at looseEqual (packages/shared/src/looseEqual.ts:64)
    ...
[Vue warn]: Unhandled error during execution of directive hook
```

### System Info
Reproduced locally with `vuejs/core@main` (5409708) via vitest: both the unit-level `looseEqual` calls and the component-level render path (same shape as the test added in #15328) throw `RangeError`.

### Any additional comments?
This is a **regression introduced by #15328** ("fix(shared): correctly compare Map and Set values", released in **v3.5.42**), which added `looseCompareCollections` in `packages/shared/src/looseEqual.ts`:

```ts
function looseCompareCollections(
  a: Map<any, any> | Set<any>,
  b: Map<any, any> | Set<any>,
) {
  if (a.size !== b.size) return false
  const candidates = Array.from(b)
  const matched = new Uint8Array(candidates.length)
  for (const item of a) {
    let index = -1
    for (let i = 0; i < candidates.length; i++) {
      if (!matched[i] && looseEqual(item, candidates[i])) {
        index = i
        break
      }
    }
    if (index < 0) return false
    matched[index] = 1
  }
  return true
}
```

`looseEqual(item, candidates[i])` recurses into each `[key, value]` pair (Map) or element (Set), so a Map/Set whose entries point back to the collection itself or to each other causes unbounded recursion. Before 3.5.42, Maps/Sets never recursed into their entries (they fell through to `String()` comparison), so this exact code path — a `<select v-model>` with Map/Set values, which is precisely the scenario #15320/#15328 added support for — **did not throw on 3.5.41**; it silently compared wrong, which #15328 fixed.

Note: #5318 covers the same root cause for cyclic plain objects (pre-existing, still open). The Map/Set case is new in 3.5.42: cyclic Maps/Sets did not throw before.

Suggested fix: make `looseEqual` cycle-safe by tracking visited `(a, b)` pairs (e.g. with a `WeakMap<object, Set<object>>` and returning `true` on re-encounter), which also fixes #5318.

Additional local repro cases that all throw `RangeError` on current main:
- `looseEqual(new Set([a1, a2]), new Set([b1, b2]))` where `a1.peer = a2; a2.peer = a1` and `b1.peer = b2; b2.peer = b1`
- `looseEqual(mapA, mapB)` where both maps hold mutually-referencing values
- `looseEqual(s1, s2)` where `s1.add(s1)` and `s2.add(s2)`
